title: Brew & Bean Profitability
prompt: Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?
interviewerNotes: Push candidate to disaggregate revenue vs. cost drivers first. If candidate jumps to solutions, redirect to diagnosis. Key insight: COGS explains 16 of the 18 points of margin decline (overhead adds the other 2; labor is flat), driven by broad input-cost inflation (about 38% across inputs) that was never passed through — menu prices have not changed in two years, and the higher average ticket is customers buying more items. Coffee beans (+40%) are the most visible driver but, at 25% of COGS, explain only about 4.2 of the 16 points; other inputs (dairy, packaging, food, up 37.5%) explain the other 11.8. If the candidate stops at beans, probe whether beans alone can explain 16 points. If candidate gets close, probe whether price elasticity was tested.

mathSteps.description: Current profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 58 - 22 - 14
Prior profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 42 - 22 - 12 = 24

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.
Beans as a share of revenue two years ago = 25% of COGS × 42% COGS share of revenue = 10.5 points
Bean inflation's contribution to the COGS increase = 10.5 points × 40% = 4.2 points of revenue

exhibits.title: Brew & Bean Cost Structure Over Time
exhibits.interpretationKey: COGS drives the margin compression: 16 of the 18 points (labor is flat; overhead adds the other 2). A strong candidate names COGS specifically, asks what's inside it, and tests whether the coffee bean spike (+40%) can explain the full 16 points — it can't: beans are 25% of COGS, so they add about 4.2 points, and other inputs up 37.5% add the other 11.8. Weak candidates say 'costs went up' without specifying, or stop at beans.

structureKey: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
recommendationKey: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.

answerKeyIdeas.idea: Lower-cost commodity blend for budget-conscious locations

structure.needs_work: Jumps to solutions or lists unrelated ideas without a profit framework. Does not disaggregate revenue vs. cost.
structure.meets_bar: Correctly uses profit = revenue − costs framework; breaks costs into major buckets; asks for data before diagnosing.
structure.strong: Proactively hypothesizes the most likely driver (cost inflation given revenue growth), structures issue tree top-down, and sizes buckets before receiving data.

quantitative.needs_work: Cannot calculate margins or makes arithmetic errors. Does not quantify the impact of COGS increase.
quantitative.meets_bar: Correctly calculates current vs. prior margin (24% → 6%) and identifies the 16pp COGS increase as the driver.
quantitative.strong: Calculates dollar impact of COGS increase (~$77M), tests whether bean inflation explains the 16pp (it explains about 4.2), cross-checks revenue per store, and synthesizes math into a clear recommendation sizing.

judgment.needs_work: Recommends blanket cost cuts or generic 'increase revenue' without testing pricing elasticity or supply-side options.
judgment.meets_bar: Identifies pricing and procurement as the two levers; acknowledges trade-offs between them.
judgment.strong: Differentiates by SKU elasticity, proposes a testable pilot, and proactively flags risks (customer churn on price increases, bean contract lock-in).

communication.needs_work: Rambles, loses the thread, or presents findings without a logical storyline.
communication.meets_bar: Communicates findings in a logical sequence; summarizes key insight clearly.
communication.strong: Uses crisp top-down communication (answer first), adapts to interviewer pushback without becoming defensive, and recaps the MECE structure after each data reveal.

synthesis.needs_work: Cannot integrate all data points into a single coherent recommendation.
synthesis.meets_bar: Connects COGS data and pricing data to a specific recommendation with rationale.
synthesis.strong: Delivers a 30-second recommendation that names the root cause, the two-lever solution, and the top risk — unprompted, at the end of the case.
